title: Imperfect or indefinido?
why: You now know the indefinido and the imperfecto; this lesson teaches you to combine them in the same sentence, using what English already does with “was …ing” and the simple past. Background and event, an interrupted action (estaba durmiendo cuando sonó el teléfono), habit or one-off fact, and the verbs that change meaning (conocí, supe, no quise): it's the key to telling stories in the past.

{"lessons": ["

The background and the event

Spanish chooses between the imperfecto and the indefinido depending on the role the action plays in the story. Think of a movie: the imperfect is the background, the setting; the indefinido is the actions that move the story forward.

Imperfecto: the backgroundIndefinido: the event
Llovía… (it was raining)… cuando salí (when I went out).
Hacía sol… (it was sunny)… y fuimos a la playa (and we went to the beach).
Había mucha gente… (there were lots of people)… y no encontramos mesa (and we didn't find a table).
Era tarde… (it was late)… y cogimos un taxi (and we took a taxi).

The background answers the questions “what was it like?”, “what was the weather like?”, “what was going on?”. The event answers “what happened?”.

Eran las once, hacía frío y las calles estaban vacías. Entonces sonó mi móvil.It was eleven o'clock, it was cold and the streets were empty. Then my phone rang.

The English speaker's trick: “was …ing” and “used to” point to the imperfect: “it was raining” → llovía. A step in the story (“what happened next?”) points to the indefinido: “it rained (all day)” → llovió. Be careful with the English simple past, which can be either: “The house was big” is background (imperfect), “I was there for two hours” is a finished event (indefinido).

", "

An interrupted action: estaba durmiendo cuando…

For an action in progress when something else happens, Spanish very often uses estar in the imperfect + gerund, exactly like English “I was sleeping”. You already know estoy durmiendo; just put estar in the imperfect.

estar + gerund
yoestaba durmiendo
túestabas durmiendo
él, ella, ustedestaba durmiendo
nosotros, nosotrasestábamos durmiendo
vosotros, vosotrasestabais durmiendo
ellos, ellas, ustedesestaban durmiendo
Estaba durmiendo cuando sonó el teléfono.I was sleeping when the phone rang.

You can also simply say Dormía cuando sonó el teléfono: both are correct. What matters is that the interrupted action is in the imperfect and the interruption in the indefinido.

Habit or one-off

Habit: imperfectoOnce: indefinido
Los domingos comíamos en casa de mi abuela.El domingo pasado comimos en un restaurante.
Siempre íbamos a la playa en coche.El verano de 2010 fuimos en tren.
De pequeño me levantaba a las siete.Ayer me levanté a las diez.

Time markers help you: siempre, todos los días, los domingos, de pequeño call for the imperfect; ayer, un día, el domingo pasado, en 2015 call for the indefinido. In English, “we would eat at my grandma's on Sundays” is a habit too: imperfect.

", "

Verbs that change meaning

A few verbs don't mean quite the same thing in the imperfect and in the indefinido. English makes the same distinction, but with different words.

VerbImperfectoIndefinido
conocerconocía a Pablo: I knew Pabloconocí a Pablo: I met Pablo
sabersabía la verdad: I knew the truthsupe la verdad: I found out the truth
tenertenía un coche: I had a cartuve un accidente: I had an accident
quererquería salir: I wanted to go outno quise salir: I refused to go out
poderpodía ir: I could gopude ir: I managed to go
Conocí a Laura en 2018, en un concierto. Entonces no sabía hablar español.I met Laura in 2018, at a concert. Back then, I couldn't speak Spanish.
Ayer supe que Jorge tenía un hermano gemelo.Yesterday I found out that Jorge had a twin brother.

English “to meet” covers two Spanish verbs. Meeting someone for the first time is conocí a + person (with the personal a). Meeting up with someone you already know is something else: vi a Marta (I saw Marta, I met up with Marta).
